question: The total linear momentum of a system of particles is found by
opt_a: adding only the speeds of all particles
opt_b: vector addition of all particle momenta
opt_c: multiplying total mass by total time
opt_d: taking the largest single momentum only
explanation: Linear momentum is a vector quantity, so total momentum must be found by vector addition. For a system, the total momentum can be written as \(\vec{P}=\vec{p}_1+\vec{p}_2+\vec{p}_3+\cdots\). If all particles move along one straight line, signs can be used to represent direction. Adding only speeds would ignore mass and direction. Taking only the largest momentum would ignore the contribution of other particles. The word “total” in momentum conservation always refers to the vector sum for the chosen system.

question: Momentum of a system is conserved when the net external force on the system is
opt_a: equal to the largest internal force
opt_c: always equal to its total mass
opt_d: opposite to every velocity in the system
explanation: Conservation of linear momentum applies to a chosen system when the net external force on that system is zero or negligible. Internal forces may act between parts of the system, but they occur in equal and opposite pairs. These internal forces cannot change the total momentum of the whole system. External forces are different because they come from bodies outside the chosen system. If the net external force is non-zero, the total momentum of the system changes with time. The condition for conservation is about net external force, not about the absence of all forces.

question: Two blocks collide on a smooth horizontal surface and are treated together as one system. During the collision, the contact force exerted by one block on the other is
opt_a: an internal force of the two-block system
opt_b: an external force of the two-block system
opt_c: the weight of the two-block system
opt_d: a force that acts on neither block
explanation: The classification of a force depends on the system chosen. If both colliding blocks are included in one system, the force between them is an interaction between parts of the same system. Such a force is internal to the two-block system. The force may change the momentum of each block separately, but it does not change the total momentum of the two-block system by itself. Weight would be a gravitational force due to Earth and is not the same as the contact force between the blocks. This system choice is the reason momentum conservation is useful in collisions.

question:
Study the table and identify the row that correctly states the conservation condition.

P\(\sum\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}=0\)Total momentum remains constant
QInternal forces are largeTotal momentum must become zero
ROne object has large massTotal momentum is always conserved
SObjects are moving fastExternal force is impossible
explanation: Row P gives the correct condition for conservation of total linear momentum. If \(\sum\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}=0\), then the total momentum of the chosen system remains constant. Large internal forces can change individual momenta strongly, but they do not by themselves change the system’s total momentum. A large mass does not automatically guarantee momentum conservation if an external force acts. High speed also does not remove the possibility of external forces. The conservation condition is decided by the net external force on the chosen system.

question: A two-particle system has momenta \(+6\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\) and \(-6\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\) along the same straight line. The total momentum of the system is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given momenta:} \) \(p_1=+6\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\) and \(p_2=-6\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\).
The signs show opposite directions along the same line.
\( \textbf{Total momentum relation:} \)
\[P=p_1+p_2\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[P=(+6)+(-6)\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[P=0\]
The two momenta cancel as vectors because they have equal magnitudes and opposite directions.
This does not mean the particles are individually at rest.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The total momentum of the system is zero.

question: A system is called isolated for momentum-conservation purposes when
opt_a: no internal interaction occurs inside it
opt_b: all bodies in it are at rest
opt_c: every body in it has zero mass
opt_d: no net external force acts on it
explanation: An isolated system, in the momentum sense, is one for which the net external force is zero or negligible. The bodies inside the system may still interact strongly with each other. Those internal forces can redistribute momentum among the bodies but cannot change the total momentum of the whole isolated system. The bodies need not be at rest; a moving isolated system can have constant total momentum. Mass does not become zero in an isolated system. The key boundary is between forces from inside the system and forces from outside it.

question: A cart of mass \(2\,\text{kg}\) moves east at \(3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), and another cart of mass \(1\,\text{kg}\) moves west at \(4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). Taking east as positive, the total momentum is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Sign convention:} \) East is positive, so west is negative.
\( \textbf{Cart 1 data:} \) \(m_1=2\,\text{kg}\), \(v_1=+3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Cart 2 data:} \) \(m_2=1\,\text{kg}\), \(v_2=-4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Momentum of cart 1:} \)
\[p_1=m_1v_1=(2)(+3)=+6\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
\( \textbf{Momentum of cart 2:} \)
\[p_2=m_2v_2=(1)(-4)=-4\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
\( \textbf{Total momentum:} \)
\[P=p_1+p_2=+6+(-4)\]
\[P=+2\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
The positive sign means the total momentum is eastward.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The total momentum is \(+2\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\).

question: A system has total momentum changing with time. The most direct conclusion is that
opt_b: all particles must have equal masses
opt_c: the system must be at rest
opt_d: a non-zero external net force acts
explanation: For a system, Newton’s second law can be written in the form \(\sum\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}=\frac{d\vec{P}}{dt}\). If the total momentum \(\vec{P}\) changes with time, then \(\frac{d\vec{P}}{dt}\) is not zero. This means the net external force is not zero. Internal forces can change the momenta of individual parts, but they do not change the total momentum of the whole system. Equal masses are not required for conservation. A system can be moving and still have constant total momentum if the net external force is zero.

question:
Consider the statements below.
I. Momentum conservation is applied to a chosen system.
II. Internal forces can change individual momenta inside the system.
III. Internal forces alone can change the total momentum of an isolated system.
The suitable set is
explanation: Statement I is suitable because momentum conservation always refers to a selected system. Statement II is also suitable because internal forces can transfer momentum from one part of the system to another. Statement III is not suitable because internal forces occur in equal and opposite pairs within the system. Their total contribution to the rate of change of system momentum cancels. For an isolated system, total momentum remains constant even though individual momenta may change. The distinction between individual momentum and total system momentum is essential here.

question: A shell explodes into two parts while floating freely in space, with no external force during the explosion. If the shell was initially at rest, the total momentum of the two parts just after explosion is
opt_a: equal to the larger part’s momentum only
opt_b: equal to the smaller part’s momentum only
explanation: The shell is the chosen system, and the explosion forces between its parts are internal. Since no external force is acting during the explosion, the total momentum of the system is conserved. The initial momentum of the shell was zero because it was at rest. Therefore the total momentum after explosion must also be zero. The two parts can move in opposite directions with equal and opposite momenta. The total momentum is not the momentum of one part alone, because the vector sum of both parts must be considered.

question: A \(3\,\text{kg}\) body moving east at \(2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) and a \(1\,\text{kg}\) body moving east at \(5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) form a system. The system’s total momentum is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Body 1 data:} \) \(m_1=3\,\text{kg}\), \(v_1=2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) east.
\( \textbf{Body 2 data:} \) \(m_2=1\,\text{kg}\), \(v_2=5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) east.
Both momenta point east, so their magnitudes add.
\( \textbf{Momentum of body 1:} \)
\[p_1=m_1v_1=(3)(2)=6\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
\( \textbf{Momentum of body 2:} \)
\[p_2=m_2v_2=(1)(5)=5\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
\( \textbf{Total momentum:} \)
\[P=p_1+p_2=6+5\]
\[P=11\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
The direction remains east because both momenta are eastward.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The total momentum is \(11\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\) east.

question: Two bodies interact only with each other in deep space. During the interaction, one body gains momentum \(+8\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\). The momentum change of the other body is
explanation: The two bodies form an isolated system because they interact only with each other. Total momentum of the system must remain constant. If one body gains \(+8\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\), the other must gain an equal change in the opposite direction. This keeps the total change in system momentum equal to zero. In symbols, \(\Delta p_1+\Delta p_2=0\). Therefore \(\Delta p_2=-\Delta p_1=-8\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\). Internal forces change individual momenta in opposite ways.

question: A system contains two carts connected by a compressed spring. The spring is released on a smooth horizontal track. Treating both carts as one system, the spring force is
opt_b: external, so it must change the total momentum of the two-cart system
opt_c: gravitational, so it acts vertically only
opt_d: absent because the track is smooth
explanation: If both carts and the spring interaction between them are considered within the same system, the spring force is internal. The spring can push the carts apart and change each cart’s momentum separately. However, the forces on the two carts are equal and opposite, so their contributions to total system momentum cancel. A smooth track reduces external horizontal forces such as friction. The spring force is not absent; it is simply internal to the chosen system. This is why the total horizontal momentum can remain conserved while the carts move apart.

question: A momentum-conservation equation is written for two bodies before and after interaction in one dimension. The correct general form is
explanation: In one-dimensional motion, momentum conservation is written by equating total initial momentum to total final momentum. The initial momenta are \(m_1u_1\) and \(m_2u_2\). The final momenta are \(m_1v_1\) and \(m_2v_2\). Therefore the suitable equation is \(m_1u_1+m_2u_2=m_1v_1+m_2v_2\), with signs chosen according to direction. The total final momentum is not always zero; it equals the initial total momentum. Adding velocities alone is not enough because mass also affects momentum.

question: The derivation of momentum conservation for two interacting bodies uses Newton’s third law mainly to show that
opt_a: external force must always be large
opt_b: both bodies must have the same acceleration
opt_c: both bodies must stop after interaction
opt_d: internal force changes cancel in total
explanation: During an interaction, body \(1\) exerts a force on body \(2\), and body \(2\) exerts an equal and opposite force on body \(1\). By Newton’s second law in momentum form, each force equals the rate of change of momentum of the body on which it acts. Because the internal forces are equal and opposite, the rates of change of the two momenta are equal and opposite. Adding them gives zero rate of change of total momentum when no net external force acts. This gives conservation of total momentum. The derivation does not require equal accelerations, because the two masses may be different.

question:
Assertion: Internal forces cannot change the total momentum of an isolated system.
Reason: Internal forces between two parts of the system occur in equal and opposite pairs.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: Internal forces act between parts of the same chosen system. Newton’s third law says that each such interaction produces equal and opposite forces on the two interacting parts. These forces can change the momentum of each part separately. However, their contributions to the total momentum change of the whole system cancel. Therefore internal forces cannot change total momentum of an isolated system. The Reason gives the mechanism by which the Assertion becomes true.

question: A two-body system has total initial momentum \(18\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\) east. During a short interaction, the net external impulse is negligible. The total final momentum is
opt_d: impossible to relate to the initial momentum
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial total momentum:} \) \(\vec{P}_i=18\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\) east.
\( \textbf{Condition:} \) Net external impulse is negligible.
Negligible external impulse means the change in total system momentum is negligible.
\( \textbf{Conservation statement:} \)
\[\vec{P}_f=\vec{P}_i\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[\vec{P}_f=18\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\text{ east}\]
Internal forces during the interaction may redistribute momentum between the two bodies.
They do not change the total momentum of the system under the stated condition.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The total final momentum is \(18\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\) east.

question:
Read the case below and answer the question.
Two carts collide on a horizontal track. In Case P, the track is smooth and the collision time is very short. In Case Q, a strong external brake acts on one cart during the collision.
Momentum conservation for the two-cart system is more reliable in
opt_c: both cases equally, regardless of the brake
opt_d: neither case because collisions never conserve momentum
explanation: Momentum conservation for a chosen system requires the net external force or external impulse to be zero or negligible during the interaction. In Case P, the smooth track and short collision time make external horizontal impulse small, so conservation is more reliable. In Case Q, the external brake applies an outside force to one cart during the collision. That external impulse can change the total momentum of the two-cart system. Collisions can conserve momentum when the proper system is chosen and external effects are negligible. The brake case shows why the conservation condition must be checked before writing the equation.

question: Two bodies of masses \(m\) and \(2m\) are initially at rest on a smooth surface. They push apart due only to an internal spring. If the body of mass \(m\) moves right with speed \(2v\), the body of mass \(2m\) moves
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial condition:} \) Both bodies are at rest, so total initial momentum is zero.
Since the spring force is internal and the surface is smooth, total momentum remains zero.
Take right as positive.
\( \textbf{Momentum of mass \(m\):} \)
\[p_1=m(2v)=2mv\]
Let the velocity of mass \(2m\) be \(V\).
\( \textbf{Conservation of momentum:} \)
\[0=2mv+(2m)V\]
\( \textbf{Solving:} \)
\[(2m)V=-2mv\]
\[V=-v\]
The negative sign means the body of mass \(2m\) moves left.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The \(2m\) body moves left with speed \(v\).

question: In a derivation using \(\sum\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}=\frac{d\vec{P}}{dt}\), if \(\sum\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}=0\), then
opt_a: every particle in the system is at rest
opt_c: total kinetic energy must be zero
explanation: The equation \(\sum\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}=\frac{d\vec{P}}{dt}\) relates the net external force on a system to the rate of change of total momentum. If \(\sum\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}=0\), then \(\frac{d\vec{P}}{dt}=0\). This means the total momentum \(\vec{P}\) does not change with time. It does not require every particle to be at rest. Internal forces may still act and may change the momenta of individual particles. Momentum conservation is a statement about the total vector momentum of the system, not about the absence of all motion.

question: A \(2\,\text{kg}\) cart moving right at \(6\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) collides with a stationary \(4\,\text{kg}\) cart. They stick together after collision on a smooth horizontal track. Their common velocity is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) \(m_1=2\,\text{kg}\), \(u_1=6\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) right, \(m_2=4\,\text{kg}\), and \(u_2=0\).
The carts stick together, so their final velocity is common; call it \(v\).
Take right as positive.
\( \textbf{Momentum conservation:} \)
\[m_1u_1+m_2u_2=(m_1+m_2)v\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[(2)(6)+(4)(0)=(2+4)v\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[12=6v\]
\( \textbf{Solving:} \)
\[v=2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\]
The positive value means the combined carts move right.
The final speed is less than \(6\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) because the same momentum is shared by a larger combined mass.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The common velocity is \(2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) right.

question: In a one-dimensional collision, taking right as positive mainly helps to
opt_a: remove mass from the conservation equation
opt_b: make all velocities positive after collision
opt_c: prove that kinetic energy is always conserved
opt_d: opposite directions are included through signs
explanation: Momentum is a vector quantity, so direction must be represented in a one-dimensional equation. Choosing right as positive automatically makes leftward velocities negative. This allows the conservation equation \(m_1u_1+m_2u_2=m_1v_1+m_2v_2\) to include direction correctly. The sign convention does not remove mass from the equation. It also does not force final velocities to be positive. Momentum conservation can be applied even when kinetic energy is not conserved, so sign choice should not be confused with an energy condition.

question: A \(5\,\text{kg}\) body moving east at \(4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) collides with a \(5\,\text{kg}\) body moving west at \(4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). If they stick together after collision, their common velocity is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Sign convention:} \) Take east as positive, so west is negative.
\( \textbf{Given:} \) \(m_1=5\,\text{kg}\), \(u_1=+4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), \(m_2=5\,\text{kg}\), and \(u_2=-4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
They stick together, so final velocity is common \(v\).
\( \textbf{Initial total momentum:} \)
\[P_i=m_1u_1+m_2u_2\]
\[P_i=(5)(+4)+(5)(-4)\]
\[P_i=20-20=0\]
\( \textbf{Final momentum:} \)
\[P_f=(m_1+m_2)v=(10)v\]
\( \textbf{Conservation:} \)
\[0=10v\]
\[v=0\]
The two initial momenta cancel because they are equal and opposite.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The stuck-together bodies remain at rest after collision.

question: A rifle of mass \(4\,\text{kg}\) fires a bullet of mass \(0.02\,\text{kg}\) with speed \(400\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) forward. If the rifle was initially at rest, its recoil speed is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial condition:} \) Rifle and bullet are initially at rest, so total initial momentum is zero.
Take the bullet’s forward direction as positive.
\( \textbf{Bullet data:} \) \(m_b=0.02\,\text{kg}\), \(v_b=+400\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Rifle data:} \) \(m_r=4\,\text{kg}\), recoil velocity \(v_r\).
\( \textbf{Momentum conservation:} \)
\[0=m_bv_b+m_rv_r\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[0=(0.02)(400)+(4)v_r\]
\( \textbf{Bullet momentum:} \)
\[(0.02)(400)=8\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
\( \textbf{Solving:} \)
\[0=8+4v_r\]
\[v_r=-2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\]
The negative sign means the rifle recoils backward.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The recoil speed is \(2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) backward.

question:

explanation:

question: A shell initially at rest explodes into two fragments of masses \(2\,\text{kg}\) and \(3\,\text{kg}\). The \(2\,\text{kg}\) fragment moves east at \(15\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). The velocity of the \(3\,\text{kg}\) fragment is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial condition:} \) The shell is initially at rest, so total initial momentum is zero.
Take east as positive.
\( \textbf{Fragment 1:} \) \(m_1=2\,\text{kg}\), \(v_1=+15\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Fragment 2:} \) \(m_2=3\,\text{kg}\), velocity \(v_2\).
\( \textbf{Momentum conservation:} \)
\[0=m_1v_1+m_2v_2\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[0=(2)(15)+(3)v_2\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[0=30+3v_2\]
\[3v_2=-30\]
\[v_2=-10\,\text{m s}^{-1}\]
The negative sign means the second fragment moves west.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The \(3\,\text{kg}\) fragment moves at \(10\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) west.

question: A moving cart collides with another cart and the two stick together. This collision is suitable for applying conservation of momentum when
opt_b: the carts must have equal masses
opt_d: the final velocity of each cart must be zero
explanation: Momentum conservation depends on the external impulse on the chosen system. If the two carts are treated as one system and external horizontal impulse is negligible, their total momentum remains constant. The carts sticking together does not prevent momentum conservation. It only tells us that the final velocity is common. Kinetic energy is generally not conserved in a sticking collision, so it should not be assumed. Equal masses are not required; the masses enter the momentum equation according to their values.

question: A \(1\,\text{kg}\) cart moving right at \(8\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) collides with a \(3\,\text{kg}\) cart moving left at \(2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). They stick together. The common velocity after collision is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Sign convention:} \) Take right as positive and left as negative.
\( \textbf{Given:} \) \(m_1=1\,\text{kg}\), \(u_1=+8\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), \(m_2=3\,\text{kg}\), and \(u_2=-2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
The carts stick together, so final velocity is common \(v\).
\( \textbf{Momentum conservation:} \)
\[m_1u_1+m_2u_2=(m_1+m_2)v\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[(1)(8)+(3)(-2)=(1+3)v\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[8-6=4v\]
\[2=4v\]
\[v=0.5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\]
The positive sign means the combined carts move right.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The common velocity is \(0.5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) right.

question: In a recoil situation, a heavy gun and a light bullet are initially at rest. After firing, the bullet has large forward speed while the gun has small backward speed mainly because
opt_a: their momenta are equal and opposite
opt_b: the gun experiences no force during firing
opt_c: momentum conservation applies only to the bullet
opt_d: the gun has no inertia after firing
explanation: Before firing, the total momentum of the gun-bullet system is zero. If external impulse is negligible during the firing interval, total momentum after firing must also be zero. Therefore the bullet and gun have equal and opposite momenta. Since the gun has much larger mass, it needs only a small backward speed to have momentum equal in magnitude to the bullet’s momentum. The bullet has small mass, so its speed is large. The forces during firing act on both bodies as a third-law pair, and momentum conservation applies to the whole system.

question:
A two-body explosion is described below.
A body initially moving east explodes into two fragments. During the short explosion, external forces are negligible. Fragment P moves east after explosion, and fragment Q moves west.
The total momentum after explosion is
opt_c: equal only to fragment P’s momentum
opt_d: opposite to the original momentum in every case
explanation: In an explosion, the forces separating the fragments are internal forces of the system. If external forces are negligible during the short time, the total momentum of the system is conserved. Since the original body was moving east, the initial total momentum was not necessarily zero. After explosion, the vector sum of the momenta of fragments P and Q must equal that original momentum. One fragment may move west, but the other may have enough eastward momentum to keep the total unchanged. Momentum conservation compares the total before and total after, not one fragment alone.

question: A \(6\,\text{kg}\) object moving east at \(5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) breaks into two pieces. One piece of mass \(2\,\text{kg}\) moves east at \(9\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). The \(4\,\text{kg}\) piece moves with velocity
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial object:} \) Total mass \(6\,\text{kg}\), velocity \(+5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) east.
Take east as positive.
\( \textbf{Initial momentum:} \)
\[P_i=(6)(5)=30\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
\( \textbf{Piece 1:} \) \(m_1=2\,\text{kg}\), \(v_1=+9\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\[p_1=(2)(9)=18\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
\( \textbf{Piece 2:} \) \(m_2=4\,\text{kg}\), velocity \(v_2\).
\( \textbf{Momentum conservation:} \)
\[P_i=p_1+m_2v_2\]
\[30=18+4v_2\]
\[4v_2=12\]
\[v_2=3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\]
The positive sign shows that the \(4\,\text{kg}\) piece also moves east.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The \(4\,\text{kg}\) piece moves at \(3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) east.

question: A student compares two methods for a sticking collision. Method P uses conservation of momentum. Method Q assumes the two bodies keep their separate velocities after sticking. The suitable method is
opt_a: Method Q, because each body must keep its original velocity
opt_b: both methods, because sticking has no effect on velocity
opt_c: Method P, because sticking gives a common final velocity
opt_d: neither method, because momentum is never conserved in collisions
explanation: In a sticking collision, the two bodies move together after collision. This means they have a common final velocity. If the net external impulse is negligible, conservation of momentum gives the equation needed to find that common velocity. Method Q is not suitable because two bodies stuck together cannot continue with two different velocities. Momentum can be conserved in collisions even when kinetic energy is not conserved. The sticking condition is a final-motion constraint, while momentum conservation gives the value of the common velocity.

question: A \(10\,\text{g}\) bullet is fired from a \(2.0\,\text{kg}\) gun. The bullet leaves at \(300\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) forward. The recoil speed of the gun is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Bullet mass conversion:} \)
\[10\,\text{g}=0.010\,\text{kg}\]
\( \textbf{Initial condition:} \) Gun and bullet are initially at rest, so total initial momentum is zero.
Take the bullet’s forward direction as positive.
\( \textbf{Bullet momentum after firing:} \)
\[p_b=(0.010)(300)\]
\[p_b=3.0\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
Let the gun recoil velocity be \(v_g\).
\( \textbf{Momentum conservation:} \)
\[0=p_b+m_gv_g\]
\[0=3.0+(2.0)v_g\]
\( \textbf{Solving:} \)
\[(2.0)v_g=-3.0\]
\[v_g=-1.5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\]
The negative sign means the gun moves backward.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The recoil speed is \(1.5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) backward.

question: A body of mass \(M\) at rest breaks into two parts of masses \(\frac{M}{4}\) and \(\frac{3M}{4}\). The smaller part moves right with speed \(6\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). The speed of the larger part is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial condition:} \) The body is at rest, so initial momentum is zero.
Take right as positive.
\( \textbf{Smaller part:} \) Mass \(=\frac{M}{4}\), velocity \(=+6\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Larger part:} \) Mass \(=\frac{3M}{4}\), velocity \(=V\).
\( \textbf{Momentum conservation:} \)
\[0=\left(\frac{M}{4}\right)(6)+\left(\frac{3M}{4}\right)V\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[0=\frac{6M}{4}+\frac{3MV}{4}\]
Multiply by \(\frac{4}{M}\):
\[0=6+3V\]
\[3V=-6\]
\[V=-2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\]
The negative sign means the larger part moves left.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The larger part moves at \(2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) left.

question:
The table below gives four proposed signs in a one-dimensional recoil problem where forward is positive.
RowBullet velocityGun recoil velocity
P\(+v_b\)\(-v_g\)
Q\(+v_b\)\(+v_g\)
R\(-v_b\)\(-v_g\)
S\(0\)\(+v_g\)
For a bullet fired forward from an initially resting gun, the suitable sign pattern is
explanation: If forward is chosen as positive, the bullet fired forward has positive velocity \(+v_b\). The gun recoils in the opposite direction, so its velocity must be negative, \(-v_g\). This sign pattern allows the final total momentum to remain zero when the initial gun-bullet system was at rest. Row Q would place both bullet and gun moving forward, giving a non-zero total momentum without an external impulse. Row R sends both backward, which does not match the stated firing direction. Row S incorrectly gives zero bullet velocity after firing.

question: A cart of mass \(m\) moving with speed \(u\) collides and sticks to an identical cart initially at rest. Their common speed is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) First cart has mass \(m\) and speed \(u\). The second identical cart has mass \(m\) and initial speed \(0\).
They stick together, so final mass moving together is \(2m\).
\( \textbf{Momentum conservation:} \)
\[mu+m(0)=(m+m)v\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[mu=2mv\]
Cancel \(m\) from both sides:
\[u=2v\]
\( \textbf{Solving:} \)
\[v=\frac{u}{2}\]
The final speed is half the original speed because the moving momentum is shared by twice the mass.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The common speed is \(\frac{u}{2}\).

question: A collision record gives total momentum before collision as \(+12\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\). After collision, body P has momentum \(+20\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\). If external impulse is negligible, body Q must have momentum
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial total momentum:} \)
\[P_i=+12\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
With negligible external impulse:
\[P_f=P_i\]
\( \textbf{Final total momentum:} \)
\[P_f=p_P+p_Q\]
\( \textbf{Given final momentum of P:} \)
\[p_P=+20\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[+12=+20+p_Q\]
\( \textbf{Solving:} \)
\[p_Q=+12-20\]
\[p_Q=-8\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
The negative sign means body Q’s final momentum is opposite to the positive direction.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) Body Q has momentum \(-8\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\).

question: A collision is analysed using the equation \(m_1u_1+m_2u_2=m_1v_1+m_2v_2\). A negative value obtained for \(v_2\) means
opt_a: body \(2\) moves in the negative direction
explanation: In one-dimensional vector equations, signs represent directions. A negative velocity does not mean negative mass or absence of motion. It means the body moves opposite to the direction chosen as positive. The momentum conservation equation remains valid if the sign convention has been used consistently. A negative final velocity can occur naturally in recoil, rebound, and opposite-direction collision problems. The magnitude of velocity is the speed, while the sign gives the direction along the chosen line.

question: A \(2\,\text{kg}\) cart moving right at \(5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) collides with a \(1\,\text{kg}\) cart moving right at \(2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). After collision, the \(2\,\text{kg}\) cart moves right at \(3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). The final velocity of the \(1\,\text{kg}\) cart is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Sign convention:} \) Take right as positive.
\( \textbf{Given:} \) \(m_1=2\,\text{kg}\), \(u_1=+5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), \(m_2=1\,\text{kg}\), \(u_2=+2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), and \(v_1=+3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
Let the final velocity of the \(1\,\text{kg}\) cart be \(v_2\).
\( \textbf{Momentum conservation:} \)
\[m_1u_1+m_2u_2=m_1v_1+m_2v_2\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[(2)(5)+(1)(2)=(2)(3)+(1)v_2\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[10+2=6+v_2\]
\[12=6+v_2\]
\[v_2=6\,\text{m s}^{-1}\]
The positive sign means the \(1\,\text{kg}\) cart moves right.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The final velocity is \(6\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) right.

question: A rocket propulsion statement says, “The rocket moves because gases push it after being expelled downward.” The statement is best understood as
opt_a: proof that momentum conservation never applies to gases
opt_b: a case where the rocket has no interaction with expelled gases
opt_c: a requirement that the ground must push the rocket upward after launch
opt_d: momentum conservation and Newton’s third law
explanation: A rocket pushes exhaust gases downward and backward. The gases exert an equal and opposite force on the rocket, so Newton’s third law is involved. Momentum reasoning also explains the motion: as gases gain momentum in one direction, the rocket gains momentum in the opposite direction when the system is considered properly. The rocket does not need the ground to push it after launch. The gases and rocket interact directly during expulsion. At this level, the idea is conceptual; detailed variable-mass equations are not needed to understand the basic propulsion mechanism.

question: A particle is in equilibrium when the vector sum of all forces acting on it is
explanation: Equilibrium of a particle means the net force on it is zero. In vector form, this is written as \(\sum\vec{F}=0\). If the net force is zero, the acceleration of the particle is zero according to Newton’s second law. The particle may be at rest or may move with uniform velocity. Equilibrium is therefore not the same as saying that no forces act on the particle. Several forces may act, but their vector sum must cancel.

question: A particle moving with constant velocity in a straight line under balanced forces is an example of
explanation: If a particle moves with constant velocity, its acceleration is zero. Since \(\sum\vec{F}=m\vec{a}\), zero acceleration means the net force is zero. This is an equilibrium condition even though the particle is not at rest. Equilibrium at rest is called static equilibrium, while equilibrium with uniform motion is called dynamic equilibrium. Motion by itself does not prove non-equilibrium. What matters is whether the velocity is changing.

question:
Assertion: A particle can be in equilibrium even when three forces act on it.
Reason: Equilibrium requires the vector sum of all forces to be zero, not the absence of forces.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: A particle can have several forces acting on it and still be in equilibrium. The condition is that the resultant of all the forces must be zero. With three forces, equilibrium is possible if the three force vectors form a closed triangle when placed head-to-tail. The Reason correctly states the general equilibrium requirement. The absence of force is only one simple way to get zero net force, not the only way. A balanced multi-force situation is still an equilibrium situation.

question:
Study the table and identify the row that correctly represents particle equilibrium in two perpendicular directions.
RowHorizontal conditionVertical condition
P\(\sum F_x=0\)\(\sum F_y=0\)
Q\(\sum F_x=ma_y\)\(\sum F_y=ma_x\)
R\(\sum F_x=v_x\)\(\sum F_y=v_y\)
S\(\sum F_x=mg\)\(\sum F_y=0\)
explanation: In two-dimensional equilibrium, the net force must be zero as a vector. This requires both perpendicular components of the net force to be zero. Therefore the conditions are \(\sum F_x=0\) and \(\sum F_y=0\). Row Q mixes horizontal force with vertical acceleration and vertical force with horizontal acceleration. Row R incorrectly connects force directly with velocity instead of acceleration. Row S may occur in one special problem only if the chosen forces produce that relation, but it is not the general equilibrium condition.

question: A particle is pulled by \(6\,\text{N}\) east and \(8\,\text{N}\) north. A third force keeps the particle in equilibrium. The third force must have magnitude and direction
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given forces:} \) \(6\,\text{N}\) east and \(8\,\text{N}\) north.
These two forces are perpendicular.
\( \textbf{Resultant of the first two forces:} \)
\[R=\sqrt{6^2+8^2}\,\text{N}\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[R=\sqrt{36+64}\,\text{N}\]
\[R=\sqrt{100}\,\text{N}=10\,\text{N}\]
The resultant points between east and north, so it is northeast.
For equilibrium, the third force must cancel this resultant.
Therefore the third force must have equal magnitude \(10\,\text{N}\) and opposite direction.
The opposite of northeast is southwest.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The third force is \(10\,\text{N}\) southwest.

question: For a particle acted on by only two forces, equilibrium is possible only when the two forces are
opt_b: equal and in the same direction
explanation: If only two forces act on a particle, their vector sum must be zero for equilibrium. This can happen only if the forces cancel each other exactly. Exact cancellation requires equal magnitudes and opposite directions. Since both forces act on the same particle, they must also be along the same straight line. Perpendicular forces cannot cancel with only two forces because their resultant would not be zero. This condition is different from Newton’s third-law pairing, because both forces here act on the same particle.

question: A small ring is pulled by two horizontal strings. One string pulls \(12\,\text{N}\) to the right and the other pulls \(12\,\text{N}\) to the left. No other horizontal force acts. The horizontal acceleration of the ring is
explanation: The two horizontal forces have equal magnitudes and opposite directions. Their vector sum in the horizontal direction is zero. Therefore \(\sum F_x=0\). From Newton’s second law, \(\sum F_x=ma_x\), so \(a_x=0\) for a particle of non-zero mass. The ring may remain at rest or continue with constant horizontal velocity depending on its initial state. Equal and opposite forces on the same particle produce balance, not acceleration.

question: A \(5\,\text{kg}\) signboard is at rest and is supported by a vertical string. Taking \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), the tension in the string is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) Mass \(m=5\,\text{kg}\), \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), and the signboard is at rest.
\( \textbf{Forces on the signboard:} \) Tension \(T\) upward and weight \(mg\) downward.
Since the signboard is at rest, it is in vertical equilibrium.
\( \textbf{Equilibrium condition:} \)
\[\sum F_y=0\]
Taking upward as positive:
\[T-mg=0\]
So,
\[T=mg\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[T=(5)(10)\,\text{N}\]
\[T=50\,\text{N}\]
The tension balances the weight because there is no vertical acceleration.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The tension is \(50\,\text{N}\).

question:
A three-force equilibrium arrangement is described below.
Three forces act on a small ring. When their vectors are placed head-to-tail in order, they form a closed triangle.
The conclusion from this arrangement is that the ring has
opt_a: non-zero acceleration in the direction of the largest force
explanation: When force vectors are placed head-to-tail and form a closed polygon, their vector sum is zero. For three forces, the closed polygon becomes a triangle. A zero vector sum means the resultant force on the ring is zero. Therefore the ring can be in equilibrium. This does not mean no forces act; it means the three forces balance one another as vectors. The largest-looking single force cannot be considered alone because equilibrium depends on the vector sum of all forces.

question: A \(20\,\text{N}\) weight is suspended by two identical strings arranged symmetrically, each making angle \(\theta\) with the vertical. If the tension in each string is \(T\), the vertical equilibrium condition is
explanation: The weight acts vertically downward with magnitude \(20\,\text{N}\). Each string has tension \(T\) along the string. Since each string makes angle \(\theta\) with the vertical, the vertical component of each tension is \(T\cos\theta\). The two strings are symmetric, so their horizontal components cancel. The vertical components together support the weight. Therefore the vertical equilibrium condition is \(2T\cos\theta=20\,\text{N}\). Using \(T\sin\theta\) would be suitable for the horizontal component in this angle convention, not the vertical component.

question: A force arrangement has \(10\,\text{N}\) upward, \(7\,\text{N}\) downward, and \(3\,\text{N}\) downward acting on the same particle. The particle is
opt_c: not describable because three forces act
opt_d: the upward and downward force sums are equal
explanation: The upward force is \(10\,\text{N}\). The total downward force is \(7\,\text{N}+3\,\text{N}=10\,\text{N}\). Since the upward and downward sums are equal, the net vertical force is zero. If no other force component acts, the total resultant force is zero. A particle can be in equilibrium under three forces when their vector sum is zero. The number of forces does not decide equilibrium; the resultant force does.

question: A particle has acceleration \(0\) at an instant. The safest conclusion is that
opt_a: the net force on it is zero
opt_c: no individual force can be acting on it
explanation: For a particle of constant mass, Newton’s second law gives \(\sum\vec{F}=m\vec{a}\). If \(\vec{a}=0\), then the net force must be zero. This does not require the velocity to be zero. A particle may move with constant non-zero velocity and still have zero acceleration. Individual forces may act and balance each other. The correct equilibrium conclusion is about resultant force, not about the absence of motion or absence of all forces.

question: A particle is acted upon by three forces in a plane. The component sums are \(\sum F_x=0\) and \(\sum F_y=5\,\text{N}\). The particle is
opt_a: not in equilibrium; net force is non-zero
opt_b: equilibrium because one component is zero
opt_c: in equilibrium only if it is initially at rest
opt_d: in equilibrium only if its mass is \(5\,\text{kg}\)
explanation: For equilibrium in a plane, both component sums must be zero. Here \(\sum F_x=0\), so the horizontal forces balance. But \(\sum F_y=5\,\text{N}\), so there is a non-zero vertical resultant force. Therefore the total force vector is not zero. A non-zero net force produces acceleration for a particle of non-zero mass. Initial rest does not create equilibrium if a resultant force is present. The component test requires all independent force components to vanish.

question: A block is pulled by \(30\,\text{N}\) east and \(40\,\text{N}\) north. A balancing force is applied. The magnitude of the balancing force is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given forces:} \) \(30\,\text{N}\) east and \(40\,\text{N}\) north.
The two forces are perpendicular.
\( \textbf{Resultant magnitude:} \)
\[R=\sqrt{30^2+40^2}\,\text{N}\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[R=\sqrt{900+1600}\,\text{N}\]
\[R=\sqrt{2500}\,\text{N}\]
\[R=50\,\text{N}\]
A balancing force must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to this resultant.
The balancing force is not \(70\,\text{N}\) because perpendicular forces do not add arithmetically.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The balancing force has magnitude \(50\,\text{N}\).

question: A body is in static equilibrium under two forces. A statement says, “The forces are equal and opposite, so they must be a Newton’s third-law pair.” The error is that
opt_b: Newton’s third law applies only to moving bodies
opt_c: equal and opposite forces can never exist
opt_d: equilibrium forces must always be perpendicular
explanation: In static equilibrium of one body, the balancing forces being considered act on that same body. Newton’s third-law forces, however, act on two different bodies involved in one interaction. Equal magnitude and opposite direction are not enough to identify a third-law pair. For example, weight and normal reaction on a resting book may balance on the book, but they are not each other’s third-law partners. The third-law partner of the normal force on the book is the force of the book on the table. Body identification is what separates balanced-force pairs from action-reaction pairs.

question: A particle is under two forces \(\vec{F}_1\) and \(\vec{F}_2\). The relation that represents two-force equilibrium is
explanation: Equilibrium requires the vector sum of all forces to be zero. If only two forces act, this condition becomes \(\vec{F}_1+\vec{F}_2=0\). This means \(\vec{F}_1=-\vec{F}_2\). The forces have equal magnitudes and opposite directions. Writing only \(\vec{F}_1=\vec{F}_2\) without the negative sign would indicate same direction if the vectors are interpreted directly. The vector equation is the cleanest form because it includes direction automatically.

question: A free-body diagram is drawn for a selected body to show
opt_a: all forces exerted by that body on other bodies
opt_c: only the path followed by the body
opt_d: only the forces acting on that body
explanation: A free-body diagram is made after choosing one body as the object of interest. The diagram shows all external forces acting on that selected body. It should not include forces exerted by the selected body on other bodies. Those forces belong to the free-body diagrams of the other bodies. Velocities and paths may be useful in a problem, but they are not forces to be drawn on the diagram. A correct free-body diagram begins by isolating the body before writing equations.

question: Use the arrangement described below: a book rests on a horizontal table. The selected body for the free-body diagram is the book. The forces that should be shown on the book are
opt_a: weight downward and normal reaction upward
opt_b: weight downward and force of book on table downward
opt_c: normal reaction upward and force of book on Earth upward
opt_d: force of table on book downward and weight upward
explanation: The selected body is the book, so only forces acting on the book should be shown. Earth exerts the weight of the book downward. The table exerts a normal reaction on the book upward. The force of the book on the table acts on the table, so it should not appear in the book’s free-body diagram. The force of the book on Earth also acts on Earth, not on the book. Correct free-body diagrams depend on the phrase “force on the selected body.”

question: A block is pulled to the right on a rough horizontal floor by an applied force, but it is still at rest. The free-body diagram of the block should include
opt_b: weight, normal, applied force, and friction
opt_d: applied force and the block’s force on the hand
explanation: The block has weight acting downward due to Earth. The floor exerts a normal reaction upward on the block. The applied pull acts to the right. Since the block is on a rough floor and tends to move right, static friction acts to the left to oppose the tendency of relative motion. Acceleration is not a force and should not be drawn as a force arrow. The force of the block on the hand acts on the hand, so it does not belong on the block’s diagram.

question: A force diagram for a block on a table includes the block’s weight \(mg\) downward, the table’s normal force \(N\) upward, and the block’s downward force on the table. The diagram is unsuitable because
opt_a: it includes the weight of the block
opt_b: it includes the normal force from the table
opt_c: it shows a force on another body
opt_d: a table cannot exert a contact force
explanation: If the selected body is the block, the diagram should include forces acting on the block. The weight \(mg\) acts on the block, so it is suitable. The normal force \(N\) from the table also acts on the block, so it is suitable. The block’s downward force on the table acts on the table, not on the block. Including that force mixes two different free-body diagrams into one. The diagram should be corrected by removing forces exerted by the block and keeping only forces acting on the block.

question: The weight of a body near Earth is the force exerted on it by
opt_a: the normal reaction of the floor
opt_c: the tension of any string nearby
explanation: Weight is the gravitational force exerted by Earth on a body. Its magnitude near Earth is commonly written as \(W=mg\), where \(m\) is the mass and \(g\) is acceleration due to gravity. Weight acts vertically downward toward Earth’s centre in ordinary near-Earth problems. It is not the same as normal reaction, which is a contact force from a surface. A body can have weight even when it is not touching any surface. The direction and source of weight should be identified before writing force equations.

question: The normal reaction exerted by a surface on a body is always directed
opt_c: opposite to the body’s velocity in every situation
opt_d: along the string attached to the body
explanation: The normal reaction is a contact force exerted by a surface on a body. The word normal means perpendicular, so the force is perpendicular to the surface at the point of contact. On a horizontal table, this direction is vertical upward. On an inclined plane, the normal reaction is tilted and perpendicular to the plane, not vertical upward. It is also different from friction, which acts along the surface. The surface orientation decides the direction of the normal reaction.

question: A light string is attached to a block and pulled. The force exerted by the string on the block is best described as
opt_a: normal reaction perpendicular to the string
opt_b: weight along the string, pushing the block
opt_c: tension along the string, pulling the block
opt_d: friction always opposite to the string
explanation: A string can pull a body along its own length. This pulling force is called tension. An ideal string is assumed light and flexible, so it transmits tension along the string direction. A string does not push a body in the way a rigid rod may push. Weight is gravitational and acts downward near Earth, not automatically along a string. The direction of tension should be drawn along the string away from the body being considered.

question:
Study the table and identify the row that correctly names the force.
RowSituationForce name
PEarth attracts a stone downwardWeight
QA horizontal table supports a book upwardFriction
RA string pulls a hanging lamp upwardNormal reaction
SA rough floor opposes slidingTension
explanation: Earth’s gravitational pull on a body is called weight, so row P is correctly named. A table supporting a book upward exerts a normal reaction, not friction. A string pulling a lamp exerts tension, not normal reaction. A rough floor opposing sliding exerts friction, not tension. Correct force naming depends on the interaction producing the force. A free-body diagram becomes clearer when each force is named by its source.

question: A \(3\,\text{kg}\) lamp hangs at rest from a vertical string. Taking \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), the tension in the string is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) Mass \(m=3\,\text{kg}\), \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), and the lamp is at rest.
The forces on the lamp are tension \(T\) upward and weight \(mg\) downward.
Since the lamp is at rest, acceleration is zero.
\( \textbf{Equilibrium condition:} \)
\[\sum F_y=0\]
Taking upward as positive:
\[T-mg=0\]
So,
\[T=mg\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[T=(3)(10)\,\text{N}\]
\[T=30\,\text{N}\]
The string tension equals the weight here because the lamp has no vertical acceleration.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The tension is \(30\,\text{N}\).

question: A block rests on a horizontal table and has no vertical acceleration. If its mass is \(4\,\text{kg}\) and \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), the normal reaction of the table is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) \(m=4\,\text{kg}\), \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), and \(a_y=0\).
The vertical forces on the block are normal reaction \(N\) upward and weight \(mg\) downward.
\( \textbf{Weight:} \)
\[mg=(4)(10)=40\,\text{N}\]
Since there is no vertical acceleration:
\[\sum F_y=0\]
Taking upward as positive:
\[N-mg=0\]
So,
\[N=mg\]
\[N=40\,\text{N}\]
This equality depends on the stated horizontal-table and zero-vertical-acceleration condition.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The normal reaction is \(40\,\text{N}\) upward.

question: A block is pressed against a vertical wall by a horizontal hand force. The wall’s normal reaction on the block is directed
opt_d: along the weight of the block
explanation: The normal reaction is perpendicular to the contact surface. For a vertical wall, the perpendicular direction is horizontal. If the block presses into the wall, the wall pushes the block outward, away from the wall. This force is not vertical, so it cannot by itself balance the weight. Any vertical support in such a situation would have to come from another force, such as friction if the wall is rough. The direction of normal reaction follows surface geometry, not the direction of gravity.

question: A smooth horizontal floor supports a \(6\,\text{kg}\) block. A horizontal force of \(18\,\text{N}\) acts on the block. Taking \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), the block’s horizontal acceleration and normal reaction are
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) \(m=6\,\text{kg}\), horizontal force \(F=18\,\text{N}\), and \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).
The floor is smooth, so there is no frictional force.
\( \textbf{Horizontal equation:} \)
\[\sum F_x=ma_x\]
\[18=(6)a_x\]
\[a_x=3\,\text{m s}^{-2}\]
\( \textbf{Vertical forces:} \) Normal reaction \(N\) upward and weight \(mg\) downward.
There is no vertical acceleration, so:
\[N-mg=0\]
\[N=mg=(6)(10)=60\,\text{N}\]
The horizontal pull decides \(a_x\), while the vertical balance decides \(N\).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(a_x=3\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) and \(N=60\,\text{N}\).

question:
Assertion: The normal reaction on a body is not always equal to its weight.
Reason: Normal reaction depends on the contact situation and the acceleration perpendicular to the surface.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_b: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_c: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
opt_d: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
explanation: The normal reaction is a contact force perpendicular to the surface. On a horizontal table with no vertical acceleration and no other vertical forces, \(N=mg\). That equality is a special case, not a universal rule. On an inclined plane, in an accelerating lift, or when another vertical force is applied, the normal reaction can differ from \(mg\). The Reason explains why the contact geometry and perpendicular acceleration matter. A force equation should decide \(N\) instead of assuming it automatically equals weight.

question: A box is placed on an inclined plane. The normal reaction of the plane on the box is
opt_b: parallel to the inclined plane downward
opt_c: equal and opposite to the box’s velocity
explanation: The normal reaction is perpendicular to the surface in contact. For an inclined plane, the surface is tilted, so the normal reaction is also tilted. It points perpendicular to the plane, not vertically upward. The component of weight perpendicular to the plane is often balanced by the normal reaction when there is no acceleration perpendicular to the plane. The component of weight parallel to the plane is a separate part of the force analysis. Treating the normal as vertical on an incline gives incorrect component equations.

question: In an ideal light string passing over an ideal smooth pulley, the tension is usually taken to be
opt_c: larger on the side with smaller mass always
opt_d: different at every point because the string is light
explanation: In the ideal model, the string is light and inextensible, and the pulley is smooth and light enough for rotational complications to be ignored. Under these assumptions, the tension is taken as the same throughout the continuous string. This simplification is used in many pulley and connected-body problems. It does not mean tension is zero; it means the same magnitude is transmitted along the string. If the pulley has friction or significant rotational inertia, the tension can be different on the two sides. The equality of tension is therefore a modelling condition, not a rule for every real string-pulley system.

question: A \(2\,\text{kg}\) mass hangs from a string and accelerates upward at \(3\,\text{m s}^{-2}\). Taking \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), the tension in the string is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) \(m=2\,\text{kg}\), upward acceleration \(a=3\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), and \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).
Forces on the mass are tension \(T\) upward and weight \(mg\) downward.
Take upward as positive.
\( \textbf{Newton’s second law:} \)
\[\sum F_y=ma\]
\( \textbf{Force equation:} \)
\[T-mg=ma\]
\( \textbf{Solving for tension:} \)
\[T=m(g+a)\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[T=2(10+3)\,\text{N}\]
\[T=26\,\text{N}\]
The tension is greater than the weight because the mass accelerates upward.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The tension is \(26\,\text{N}\).

question: A \(2\,\text{kg}\) mass hangs from a string and accelerates downward at \(3\,\text{m s}^{-2}\). Taking \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), the tension in the string is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) \(m=2\,\text{kg}\), downward acceleration \(a=3\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), and \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).
Take downward as positive to match the acceleration direction.
Forces are weight \(mg\) downward and tension \(T\) upward.
\( \textbf{Newton’s second law:} \)
\[\sum F_y=ma\]
\( \textbf{Force equation:} \)
\[mg-T=ma\]
\( \textbf{Solving for tension:} \)
\[T=m(g-a)\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[T=2(10-3)\,\text{N}\]
\[T=14\,\text{N}\]
The tension is less than the weight because the mass accelerates downward.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The tension is \(14\,\text{N}\).

question: A weighing scale under a person reads the normal reaction \(N\). A \(60\,\text{kg}\) person stands in a lift accelerating upward at \(2\,\text{m s}^{-2}\). Taking \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), the scale reading is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) \(m=60\,\text{kg}\), lift acceleration \(a=2\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) upward, and \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).
The scale reading is the normal reaction \(N\), not the mass.
Forces on the person are \(N\) upward and \(mg\) downward.
Take upward as positive.
\( \textbf{Newton’s second law:} \)
\[N-mg=ma\]
\( \textbf{Solving:} \)
\[N=m(g+a)\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[N=60(10+2)\,\text{N}\]
\[N=720\,\text{N}\]
The reading is greater than the usual weight because the lift accelerates upward.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The scale reads \(720\,\text{N}\).

question: A \(60\,\text{kg}\) person stands on a weighing scale in a lift accelerating downward at \(2\,\text{m s}^{-2}\). Taking \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), the scale reading is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) \(m=60\,\text{kg}\), downward acceleration \(a=2\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), and \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).
The scale reading equals the normal reaction \(N\).
Take downward as positive for the equation.
Forces on the person are weight \(mg\) downward and normal reaction \(N\) upward.
\( \textbf{Newton’s second law:} \)
\[mg-N=ma\]
\( \textbf{Solving for \(N\):} \)
\[N=m(g-a)\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[N=60(10-2)\,\text{N}\]
\[N=480\,\text{N}\]
The reading is less than the usual weight because the person and lift accelerate downward together.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The scale reads \(480\,\text{N}\).

question: A lift cable breaks and the lift falls freely. For a person inside, the apparent weight becomes zero because
opt_a: the actual gravitational force becomes zero
explanation: Apparent weight is measured by the normal reaction from the supporting surface. In free fall, the lift, floor, and person all accelerate downward with acceleration \(g\). The floor no longer needs to push up on the person to produce a different acceleration. Therefore the normal reaction becomes zero in the ideal free-fall case. The person’s actual weight \(mg\) is still present and acts downward. The feeling of weightlessness comes from zero support force, not from the disappearance of gravity.

question:
Read the case below and answer the question.
A weighing scale is placed in a lift. In Case P, the lift moves upward with constant velocity. In Case Q, the lift accelerates upward. The same person stands on the scale in both cases.
The scale reading in Case Q compared with Case P is
opt_c: equal in both cases because the person’s mass is unchanged
explanation: A scale reads the normal reaction on the person. In Case P, the lift moves with constant velocity, so acceleration is zero and \(N=mg\). In Case Q, the lift accelerates upward, so the force equation is \(N-mg=ma\). This gives \(N=m(g+a)\), which is greater than \(mg\). The person’s mass is unchanged in both cases, but the scale reading is a force, not the mass itself. Apparent weight changes when the support force changes due to acceleration.

question:
The table below lists lift situations for a person standing on a scale.
RowLift motionScale reading
PAt rest\(mg\)
QMoving upward with constant velocity\(mg\)
RAccelerating upward with acceleration \(a\)\(m(g+a)\)
SAccelerating downward with acceleration \(a\)\(m(g+a)\)
The row with an unsuitable scale reading is
explanation: At rest, the person has zero acceleration, so the normal reaction is \(mg\). Moving upward with constant velocity also means zero acceleration, so the reading remains \(mg\). For upward acceleration \(a\), the normal reaction becomes \(m(g+a)\). For downward acceleration \(a\), the force equation gives \(N=m(g-a)\), not \(m(g+a)\). Therefore row S has the unsuitable reading. The scale reading depends on acceleration, not merely on whether the lift is moving up or down.

question: A lift accelerates downward with acceleration equal to \(g\). The scale reading of a person inside is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Condition:} \) The lift accelerates downward with \(a=g\).
For a person on the scale, apparent weight equals the normal reaction \(N\).
For downward acceleration:
\[N=m(g-a)\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[N=m(g-g)\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[N=0\]
The person and scale are in free fall together, so the scale cannot exert an upward support force in the ideal case.
Actual gravitational force \(mg\) still acts downward on the person.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The scale reading is \(0\).

question: A claim says, “If a weighing scale reads \(0\), the person has no weight.” The correct interpretation in a freely falling lift is that
opt_a: apparent weight is zero, but \(mg\) still acts
opt_b: both mass and gravitational weight become zero
opt_c: the person is outside Earth’s gravitational field
opt_d: normal reaction becomes twice the weight
explanation: A weighing scale reads the normal reaction exerted by the scale on the person. In a freely falling lift, the normal reaction becomes zero, so the apparent weight is zero. However, Earth’s gravitational force on the person is still \(mg\). This gravitational force is what causes the person and lift to fall. The person’s mass is also unchanged. The phrase “weightlessness” in this case refers to loss of support force, not loss of gravity.

question: Friction is a contact force that acts mainly to oppose
opt_a: the mass of a body in all situations
opt_d: the normal reaction at every point by becoming perpendicular to it
explanation: Friction acts between surfaces in contact. It opposes actual relative motion when surfaces slide over each other. It can also oppose the tendency of relative motion when sliding has not yet started. This is why a block can remain at rest even when a small horizontal force is applied to it. Friction acts along the contact surface, not perpendicular to it. The perpendicular contact force is the normal reaction, while friction is the tangential contact force.

question: A block on a rough horizontal table is pushed gently toward the right but does not move. The friction force on the block acts
explanation: The applied push tends to make the block move toward the right. Since the block does not move, static friction adjusts itself to oppose that tendency. Therefore the friction force on the block acts toward the left. This friction is not kinetic friction because there is no sliding yet. The normal reaction acts vertically upward, and weight acts vertically downward. The direction of static friction is decided by the tendency of relative motion at the contact surface.

question: Static friction differs from kinetic friction because static friction
opt_a: is always zero when a force is applied
opt_b: acts only on bodies moving through air
opt_c: is always larger than the normal reaction
opt_d: can adjust up to a limiting value
explanation: Static friction acts when there is no relative sliding between surfaces. Its value is not fixed at one number; it adjusts to match the applied tangential force as long as slipping does not occur. It can increase only up to a maximum value called limiting friction. Once sliding begins, kinetic friction acts instead. Kinetic friction is usually approximately constant for a given normal reaction and pair of surfaces. The adjustable nature of static friction is why a small push may not start motion.

question:
Study the table and identify the row that correctly describes a friction type.
RowSituationFriction type
PA box is pushed but remains at restStatic friction
QA box slides on a rough floorStatic friction only
RA rolling ball has no contact with the groundKinetic friction
SA book presses a table verticallyTension
explanation: Row P is suitable because the box is at rest while a tangential force tries to make it move, so static friction can act. Row Q is unsuitable because a sliding box experiences kinetic friction, not only static friction. Row R is unsuitable as written because a rolling ball is still in contact with the ground, and rolling friction is a separate contact effect. Row S is not about friction at all; a book pressing a table involves contact forces such as normal reaction. The friction type should be identified from whether slipping is absent, about to occur, or already occurring.

question: A \(10\,\text{kg}\) block rests on a rough horizontal surface. If \(\mu_s=0.40\) and \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), the limiting friction is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) \(m=10\,\text{kg}\), \(\mu_s=0.40\), and \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).
On a horizontal surface with no vertical acceleration:
\[N=mg\]
\( \textbf{Normal reaction:} \)
\[N=(10)(10)=100\,\text{N}\]
\( \textbf{Limiting friction relation:} \)
\[f_{s,\max}=\mu_s N\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[f_{s,\max}=(0.40)(100\,\text{N})\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[f_{s,\max}=40\,\text{N}\]
This is the maximum possible static friction, not necessarily the actual friction for every applied force.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The limiting friction is \(40\,\text{N}\).

question: A \(10\,\text{kg}\) block has limiting friction \(40\,\text{N}\) on a horizontal rough floor. A horizontal force of \(25\,\text{N}\) is applied, but the block remains at rest. The friction force is
opt_d: zero because friction acts only during sliding
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) Maximum static friction is \(40\,\text{N}\), and the applied force is \(25\,\text{N}\).
The block remains at rest, so the net horizontal force must be zero.
Static friction adjusts to balance the applied force as long as the required value does not exceed the limiting friction.
Here the required friction is \(25\,\text{N}\).
Since \(25\,\text{N} \lt 40\,\text{N}\), static friction can provide this value.
It acts opposite to the applied force because it opposes the tendency of motion.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The friction force is \(25\,\text{N}\) opposite the applied force.

question: The coefficient of friction \(\mu\) is dimensionless because it is defined as the ratio of
explanation: The coefficient of friction is commonly defined by relations such as \(f_{s,\max}=\mu_sN\) and \(f_k=\mu_kN\). Therefore \(\mu\) is a ratio of frictional force to normal reaction. Both friction and normal reaction are forces, so both have the same SI unit \( \text{N} \). Their ratio has no unit and no dimension. This does not mean \(\mu\) has no physical meaning; it describes the nature of the pair of surfaces in contact. A unit attached to \(\mu\) would signal a mistaken interpretation of the ratio.

question:
Assertion: The actual value of static friction can be less than \(\mu_sN\).
Reason: \(\mu_sN\) represents the maximum static friction just before slipping.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_b: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_c: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: Static friction is self-adjusting as long as there is no sliding. If the applied tangential force is small, static friction takes only the value needed to maintain rest. The expression \(\mu_sN\) gives the limiting value, not the compulsory value at all times. When the required friction exceeds this maximum, sliding begins. The Reason correctly explains why the actual static friction can be smaller than \(\mu_sN\). Treating \(f_s=\mu_sN\) always is a common source of wrong force equations.

question:
A graph description is given below.
For a block at rest on a rough horizontal surface, the applied horizontal force is slowly increased from zero. The static friction force first increases with the applied force, then reaches a maximum value.
The maximum value on this graph represents
explanation: While the block remains at rest, static friction adjusts to oppose the applied force. As the applied force is slowly increased, the required static friction also increases. It cannot increase beyond its maximum possible value. This maximum value is called limiting friction and is given by \(f_{s,\max}=\mu_sN\). Once the applied force exceeds this value, the block starts sliding and kinetic friction becomes relevant. The graph shows the adjustable nature of static friction before motion begins.

question: A \(5\,\text{kg}\) block slides on a rough horizontal surface with \(\mu_k=0.20\). Taking \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), the kinetic friction is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) \(m=5\,\text{kg}\), \(\mu_k=0.20\), and \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).
On a horizontal surface with no vertical acceleration:
\[N=mg\]
\( \textbf{Normal reaction:} \)
\[N=(5)(10)=50\,\text{N}\]
\( \textbf{Kinetic friction relation:} \)
\[f_k=\mu_kN\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[f_k=(0.20)(50\,\text{N})\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[f_k=10\,\text{N}\]
Kinetic friction acts opposite to the relative sliding direction.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The kinetic friction is \(10\,\text{N}\).

question: For dry solid surfaces in the simple friction model, kinetic friction is usually
opt_a: exactly proportional to the colour of the surface
opt_c: nearly independent of apparent contact area
opt_d: zero whenever the body has mass
explanation: In the simple laws of dry friction, friction is taken to be proportional to the normal reaction. It is usually treated as approximately independent of the apparent area of contact for the same pair of surfaces and same normal reaction. This is a model for ordinary dry surfaces, not a statement about every microscopic contact situation. Kinetic friction is generally less than limiting static friction for the same surfaces. Friction is not decided by colour alone. The normal reaction and nature of the surfaces are the main quantities in the elementary model.

question: A \(4\,\text{kg}\) block is pulled horizontally by \(30\,\text{N}\) on a rough horizontal surface. If \(\mu_k=0.25\) and \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), the acceleration during sliding is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) \(m=4\,\text{kg}\), applied force \(F=30\,\text{N}\), \(\mu_k=0.25\), and \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).
\( \textbf{Normal reaction:} \)
\[N=mg=(4)(10)=40\,\text{N}\]
\( \textbf{Kinetic friction:} \)
\[f_k=\mu_kN\]
\[f_k=(0.25)(40)=10\,\text{N}\]
Friction opposes sliding, so it acts opposite to the pull.
\( \textbf{Net horizontal force:} \)
\[\sum F=30\,\text{N}-10\,\text{N}=20\,\text{N}\]
\( \textbf{Acceleration:} \)
\[a=\frac{\sum F}{m}\]
\[a=\frac{20\,\text{N}}{4\,\text{kg}}\]
\[a=5\,\text{m s}^{-2}\]
The applied force is not used alone because friction reduces the resultant force.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The acceleration is \(5\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).

question: A block slides to the right on a rough horizontal surface while no external horizontal push is applied. The friction force and acceleration are
opt_c: friction toward the right and acceleration toward the left
opt_d: friction vertically upward and acceleration toward the right
explanation: Since the block is sliding to the right, kinetic friction acts opposite to the relative sliding. Therefore the friction force on the block is toward the left. If no other horizontal force acts, this leftward friction is the net horizontal force. The acceleration is in the direction of the net force, so it is also toward the left. The block may still be moving right while accelerating left, which means it is slowing down. This separates the direction of velocity from the direction of acceleration.

question:
Match the friction expression with its meaning.
ExpressionMeaning
P. \(f_s\leq \mu_sN\)1. Static friction can adjust up to a maximum
Q. \(f_{s,\max}=\mu_sN\)2. Limiting static friction
R. \(f_k=\mu_kN\)3. Kinetic friction during sliding
S. \(\mu=\frac{f}{N}\)4. Coefficient as force ratio
The suitable matching is
explanation: The relation \(f_s\leq \mu_sN\) shows that static friction can take a range of values up to a maximum. The equality \(f_{s,\max}=\mu_sN\) represents limiting friction just before sliding begins. The relation \(f_k=\mu_kN\) is used after sliding has started. The expression \(\mu=\frac{f}{N}\) shows why coefficient of friction is a ratio of two forces. Each expression belongs to a different stage or meaning, so replacing the inequality by equality everywhere gives wrong results. The inequality in static friction is the most important distinction in the set.

question:
Read the case below and answer the question.
A box rests on a rough floor. A student applies horizontal forces of \(5\,\text{N}\), \(10\,\text{N}\), and \(15\,\text{N}\) in three trials. In all three trials, the box remains at rest. The limiting friction is \(18\,\text{N}\).
The friction force in the \(15\,\text{N}\) trial is
opt_c: zero because the box does not move
explanation: The box remains at rest in the \(15\,\text{N}\) trial, so the net horizontal force is zero. Static friction adjusts to balance the applied force as long as the needed value is within its maximum limit. The needed value is \(15\,\text{N}\). Since \(15\,\text{N}\lt18\,\text{N}\), static friction can supply this value without slipping. It acts opposite to the applied force because it opposes the tendency of relative motion. The limiting value is not used as the actual friction unless the box is just about to slip.

question: A \(2\,\text{kg}\) block slides on a rough horizontal plane with initial speed \(8\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). If \(\mu_k=0.20\) and \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), the magnitude of its deceleration is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) \(m=2\,\text{kg}\), \(\mu_k=0.20\), and \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).
The initial speed is not needed to find the frictional acceleration magnitude.
\( \textbf{Normal reaction:} \)
\[N=mg=(2)(10)=20\,\text{N}\]
\( \textbf{Kinetic friction:} \)
\[f_k=\mu_kN\]
\[f_k=(0.20)(20)=4\,\text{N}\]
This friction is the only horizontal force and acts opposite the motion.
\( \textbf{Acceleration magnitude:} \)
\[a=\frac{f_k}{m}\]
\[a=\frac{4\,\text{N}}{2\,\text{kg}}\]
\[a=2\,\text{m s}^{-2}\]
The result can also be written as \(a=\mu_kg\) for this horizontal case.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The deceleration magnitude is \(2\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).

question: A rough-surface claim says, “Static friction always acts opposite to the applied force.” The best correction is
opt_a: static friction always acts in the direction of velocity
opt_c: static friction is always equal to \(\mu_kN\)
opt_d: static friction acts only when the body is sliding
explanation: Static friction is decided by the tendency of relative motion at the contact surface. In many simple pushing examples, this direction is opposite to the applied force. However, that is not the deepest rule. For example, in walking, the ground’s static friction on the foot can act forward, helping the person move ahead. Static friction acts without sliding, while kinetic friction acts during sliding. The correct direction rule must refer to relative motion tendency between surfaces, not only to the direction of one applied force.

question: A block is kept at rest on a rough horizontal floor by static friction. If the applied force is slowly increased until the block is just about to move, then at that instant
explanation: Static friction can vary from zero up to a maximum value. The maximum value is called limiting friction. When the block is just about to move, static friction has reached this limiting value. Therefore \(f_s=f_{s,\max}=\mu_sN\) at that instant. Before this limiting condition, the actual static friction may be smaller than \(\mu_sN\). Kinetic friction becomes relevant only after sliding begins, so \(\mu_kN\) should not be used for the just-about-to-slip state.

question: For the same pair of surfaces and same normal reaction, the usual comparison between limiting static friction and kinetic friction is
opt_a: limiting static friction is greater than kinetic friction
opt_b: kinetic friction is greater than limiting static friction
opt_d: both are unrelated to the normal reaction
explanation: For most ordinary dry surfaces, the coefficient of static friction is greater than the coefficient of kinetic friction. This means \(\mu_s\gt\mu_k\). Since \(f_{s,\max}=\mu_sN\) and \(f_k=\mu_kN\), limiting static friction is usually greater than kinetic friction for the same normal reaction. This is why it often takes more force to start sliding than to keep sliding. The comparison is based on the same surface pair and same normal reaction. Changing either surface condition or \(N\) changes the numerical forces.

question: A \(6\,\text{kg}\) block is pushed horizontally with \(25\,\text{N}\) on a rough floor. The coefficients are \(\mu_s=0.50\) and \(\mu_k=0.30\), with \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\). What happens initially?
opt_a: The block moves with kinetic friction \(18\,\text{N}\)
opt_b: The block remains at rest, and static friction is \(25\,\text{N}\)
opt_c: The block moves with acceleration \(1\,\text{m s}^{-2}\)
opt_d: The block remains at rest, and static friction is \(30\,\text{N}\)
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) \(m=6\,\text{kg}\), applied force \(F=25\,\text{N}\), \(\mu_s=0.50\), \(\mu_k=0.30\), and \(g=10\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).
\( \textbf{Normal reaction:} \)
\[N=mg=(6)(10)=60\,\text{N}\]
\( \textbf{Maximum static friction:} \)
\[f_{s,\max}=\mu_sN\]
\[f_{s,\max}=(0.50)(60)=30\,\text{N}\]
The applied force needed to be balanced is \(25\,\text{N}\).
Since \(25\,\text{N}\lt30\,\text{N}\), static friction can balance the push.
Therefore the block does not start moving initially.
The actual static friction is \(25\,\text{N}\), not the maximum \(30\,\text{N}\).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The block remains at rest with static friction \(25\,\text{N}\).
